newsitem.title: JAPAN: Market view on low JGB yields unjustified--MOF.
newsitem.headline: Market view on low JGB yields unjustified--MOF.

text.p: Market expectations that reform of Japan's public financing system may lead to a fall in long-term Japanese government bond yields cannot be justified, a senior official at the Ministry of Finance (MOF) said on Wednesday.
"Such market expectations are unrealistic because in Japan the JGB futures market (which reflects economic fundamentals) is much bigger than the cash market," the official told Reuters.

Reform aimed at cutting spending in Japan's fiscal investment and loan programme (FILP), which is managed by MOF, is expected to encourage MOF to buy JGBs instead of making loans to government-affiliated agencies.
The reform was proposed by an official panel on Wednesday and is due to be finalised by the end of this calendar year.
The panel said on Wednesday that FILP spending for the fiscal year starting next April should be cut from the current 1997/98 fiscal year, although it failed to propose a target.
In a news conference on Wednesday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka questioned whether setting numerical targets would be an effective way of approaching reforms.
"We will continue to seek stream-lining (of FILP). That is the most I can say," he said when asked whether next year's planned cuts would exceed this year's three percent reduction.

The reform proposals, to be submitted to MOF and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPT), also called for extending no new loans to the financially troubled Japan National Railway Settlement Corp (JNRSC) and Japan's Forestry Agency.
The balance of loans by FILP to the JNRSC totalled 15.4 trillion yen as of end-March 1996, while those to the Forestry Agency totalled 3.3 trillion yen, another MOF official said.
"FILP should no longer make loans so readily to those whose ability to repay is in doubt," Masaaki Homma, a representative of the panel, told a news conference.
"A political decision should be made on how to deal with these two agencies' problem loans," he said.
The panel's proposals would also require FILP's borrowers to issue bonds without guarantees from the government.
"The borrowers need exposure to market discipline by issuing bonds," Homma said.

FILP, dubbed Japan's second national budget because of its massive size and semi-governmental status, takes deposits from the MPT and the Welfare Ministry and uses them to fund government-affiliated financial institutions and other quasi-governmental bodies.
As of March 1996, FILP's loans outstanding to such institutions totalled 356 trillion yen.
